summary:
AstroRelic is an interactive educational web application that brings the scientific legacy of NASA's abandoned and retired space hardware to life. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge,  Abandoned but not Forgotten, it reveals the stories behind equipment left on the Moon and Mars, showing how these missions continue to shape our understanding of space long after their operations have ended.

Through 17 mission stories, students can explore NASA imagery, narrated explanations with transcripts, interactive 3D spacecraft models, planetary globes, and a searchable mission timeline. Each story connects a spacecraft or instrument to the measurements it collected, the discoveries it enabled, and its lasting scientific contributions. Interactive quizzes, spacecraft scale comparisons, classroom activities, and educational Moon and Mars simulations make learning engaging and accessible.

By transforming scattered mission records into an interactive, source-backed learning experience, AstroRelic bridges the gap between space exploration history and modern scientific discovery. It inspires young learners to recognize that while a mission may end, its contribution to science lives on.
details:
AstroRelic: Left on Another World is a browser-based learning experience for students, teachers, and curious explorers. It addresses the challenge by telling the stories of equipment left on the Moon and Mars: why it was sent, how it worked, what it discovered, and what remains. Additional retired missions show how this scientific legacy extends across the solar system.

The archive contains 17 mission stories. Visitors can explore by story, location, or time, then open a mission page with historical context, NASA imagery, narrated explanations and transcripts, an interactive hardware viewer, a mission timeline, a planned-versus-actual comparison, and a short knowledge check. A four-step evidence trail connects hardware, measurement, discovery, and impact, helping students understand how an instrument becomes a source of scientific knowledge.

Interactive Moon and Mars globes connect mission stories to sourced locations. Regional references are clearly distinguished from precise landing coordinates. Spacecraft scale comparisons help students understand physical dimensions, while mission-design challenges and printable classroom activities connect exploration to scientific questions.

Two educational simulations add experiential learning. Students can drive a lunar rover across uneven terrain or fly and land a fictional booster-powered Mars vehicle. Keyboard and touch controls support desktop and mobile use. Gravity, momentum, collisions, rover suspension, fuel, and landing conditions introduce engineering ideas. These are educational approximations on fictional terrain, not validated spacecraft models or reconstructions of actual mission operations.

The application uses JavaScript, HTML, CSS, React, Vite, and Three.js/WebGL, with GitHub for source control hosting and Vercel for deployment. Thirteen official NASA 3D assets support fifteen archive entries; the Apollo rover and ALSEP use labelled educational reconstructions. NASA mission records, imagery, scientific reports, planetary maps, and reference values inform the content. No specialist hardware is needed beyond a compatible computer or phone.

The creative contribution is the connection between narrative and exploration: students can read about an instrument, inspect its spacecraft, locate its mission, and follow the evidence behind a discovery. Our intended impact is stronger scientific curiosity and a clearer understanding of the lasting value of space exploration. We considered source accuracy, age-appropriate explanations, mobile usability, keyboard access, reduced motion, transcripts, and limited bandwidth. Heavy 3D assets load on demand, and an inline rocket loader gives feedback during startup.

OpenAI Codex assisted with development, explanatory text and narration drafts, source research, and testing. Narration was synthesized locally using Kokoro-82M and is labelled AI-generated; it is not an astronaut recording. Scientific claims are linked to external sources, and fictional simulations and reconstructed models are identified explicitly.
